introduction: Words must be supported by deeds: the guide says it in a hundred ways, to individuals, to communities and to those who teach. A hundred of its quotations are read here with a hundred from elsewhere, and few themes have wider agreement. James asks to be shown faith by works; Jesus speaks of fruits, of the son who said yes and did not go, of those who say ‘Lord, Lord’; the prophets refuse worship without justice; the Qur’an asks why you say what you do not do; Confucius acts before he speaks; the Dhammapada compares fine words without deeds to a flower without scent; Marcus Aurelius tells himself to stop describing the good man and be one. The contrasts are placed where the guide is most absolute. Paul says a person is justified by faith without the deeds of the law, and that salvation is not of works; Isaiah calls our righteousness filthy rags; the Pharisee’s deeds stand between him and God; and Jesus, Proverbs and Dickinson insist that words are themselves acts, by which a person is justified or condemned. They do not weaken the guide’s demand, but they ask what kind of deed, done in what spirit, it is asking for.
questions: James says faith without works is dead and Paul that we are justified by faith without the deeds of the law. How does the guide's teaching that recognition comes first, and deeds must follow, stand between them?
The Pharisee in the parable has many good deeds to report. What makes a deed 'purely for God', and how would you know it in yourself?
Jesus says we shall give account of every idle word. In what ways are words themselves deeds?
Portia finds it easier to teach twenty than to be one of the twenty. Where is the gap between your own knowing and doing widest, and why?
The guide says that in this age teaching is by deeds. Think of someone who persuaded you by how they lived: what did you see?
Marcus Aurelius tells himself to stop talking about the good man and be one. What single practice would move one of your convictions from speech into action this week?

outside.why: James makes deeds the test in the same way: shew me thy faith without thy works, and I will shew thee my faith by my works.
Confucius says that he once heard men's words and gave them credit for their conduct, and now hears their words and looks at their conduct.
Jesus, having given an example, tells his disciples: if ye know these things, happy are ye if ye do them.
Aristotle observes that most people do not do the acts but take refuge in theory and think they are being philosophers.
James asks what it profits to say 'be ye warmed and filled' to the naked and hungry, and give them nothing.
Shakespeare has a mother tell her son that action is eloquence, and that the eyes of the ignorant are more learned than their ears.
James puts it as a command: be ye doers of the word, and not hearers only, deceiving your own selves.
Chaucer's parson gave his flock this example, that first he wrought and afterward he taught.
Paul says that the kingdom of God is not in word, but in power.
Jesus gives the same proof for the tree of a human life: ye shall know them by their fruits.
Proverbs says that in all labour there is profit, but the talk of the lips tends only to penury.
The Qur'an puts the demand as a question to believers: why say ye that which ye do not?
Jesus tells of two sons, one who said he would not go to the vineyard and went, and one who said he would and did not.
The Qur'an tells some who say 'we believe' to say instead 'we submit', for faith has not yet entered their hearts.
James concludes that as the body without the spirit is dead, so faith without works is dead also.
Paul concludes that a man is justified by faith without the deeds of the law. How have Christians held his sentence together with James's, and how does the guide?
Hebrews puts recognition first as well: without faith it is impossible to please God, for whoever comes must believe that he is.
Paul says that salvation is the gift of God, not of works, lest any man should boast. If deeds are not accepted without recognition, what are deeds for?
The Qur'an speaks of the greatest losers by their works: those whose effort goes astray while they reckon that they do good. Can sincere good deeds be worth nothing, and who is to say?
Paul asks the teacher of others whether he does not teach himself, and the preacher against stealing whether he steals.
Paul says that not the hearers of the law are just before God, but the doers of the law.
Jesus says that not every one who says 'Lord, Lord' shall enter the kingdom, but he that does the will of his Father.
Jesus warns against doing alms before men, to be seen of them. If a deed is to be done purely for God, can it also be the proof others look for?
A saying of Muhammad holds that the reward of deeds depends upon the intentions, each person receiving according to what was intended.
Proverbs honours the right word too: a word fitly spoken is like apples of gold in pictures of silver.
Lincoln said at Gettysburg that the world would little note what was said there, but could never forget what was done.
Jesus asks his followers to let their light so shine that others may see their good works.
Peter's letter imagines a person won without the word, by beholding the conduct of another.
Whitman says that he and his do not convince by arguments, similes or rhymes: they convince by their presence.
Paul asks for a circumspect walk that redeems the time, because the days are evil.
Paul tells Titus to show himself in all things a pattern of good works.
Hamlet's advice to the players serves for more than the stage: suit the action to the word, the word to the action.
Paul asks Timothy to be an example of the believers in word, in conduct, in charity, in spirit, in faith, in purity.
Aristotle holds that persuasion is achieved by the speaker's personal character, since we believe good men more fully and more readily.
Portia says it is a good divine that follows his own instructions, and that she could easier teach twenty than be one of the twenty. Why is the gap between knowing and doing so hard to close?
Confucius says of the superior man that he acts before he speaks, and afterwards speaks according to his actions.
Paul asks that whatever is done be done heartily, as to the Lord and not unto men.
In the parable the good ground is those who keep the word and bring forth fruit with patience.
John's letter asks his children not to love in word, neither in tongue, but in deed and in truth.
In the parable love for a stranger of another people is shown by binding wounds and paying at the inn.
Jesus asks: why call ye me Lord, Lord, and do not the things which I say?
The Qur'an says that of mankind are some who say 'we believe in God and the Last Day', when they believe not.
Jesus compares those who appear righteous outwardly to whited sepulchres, beautiful without and full of dead men's bones.
Paul says that to speak with the tongues of men and of angels without charity is to be sounding brass or a tinkling cymbal.
Confucius says that the superior man wishes to be slow in his speech and earnest in his conduct.
The Dhammapada likens the fine but fruitless words of one who does not act to a beautiful flower, full of colour, without scent.

Hamlet says that resolution is sicklied over with the pale cast of thought, and enterprises lose the name of action. Is it too much talk that keeps ideals from being carried out, or too much thinking?
Marcus Aurelius tells himself no longer to talk about the kind of man a good man ought to be, but to be such.
Carlyle's precept is to do the duty which lies nearest, and the second duty will already have become clearer.
Philip answers a friend's doubt with an invitation to verify: come and see.
Ezekiel is told that the people hear his words as a very lovely song, for they hear them and do them not.
Jesus compares the one who hears his sayings and does them to a wise man who built his house upon a rock.
Isaiah hears the complaint that this people draw near with their mouth and honour with their lips, while their heart is far away.
The Dhammapada likens the one who recites much and does not act to a cowherd counting the cows of others.
The Qur'an gives the command in one word: Act! God will behold your actions.
Longfellow's stanza is all imperative: act, act in the living present, heart within and God overhead.
Theodore Roosevelt gave the credit to the man who is actually in the arena, who strives valiantly and comes short again and again.
The psalmist asks what he shall render unto the Lord for all his benefits, and answers with vows paid in the presence of the people.
Micah says that what the Lord requires is to do justly, to love mercy and to walk humbly with thy God.
Amos hears God say that he hates and despises the feast days, and will not accept the offerings.
Jesus says that men shall give account of every idle word, and that by thy words thou shalt be justified or condemned. Are words then a kind of deed, and not its opposite?
Proverbs says that death and life are in the power of the tongue. If speech can do so much, in what sense has speech without action no effect?
Douglass recognised the widest possible difference between the Christianity of his land and the Christianity of Christ.
Micah condemns priests who teach for hire and prophets who divine for money, and still lean upon the Lord.
The Qur'an asks whether people imagine they will be left at ease because they say 'we believe', and will not be tested.
In the Gospel the deeds that count are plain ones: I was an hungred and ye gave me meat, I was sick and ye visited me.
Paul speaks of those who profess that they know God, but in works deny him.
John the Baptist warns that every tree which brings not forth good fruit is hewn down.
Paul says that the true belonging is that of the heart, in the spirit and not in the letter, whose praise is not of men.
Moses asks that the words be taught to children at home and by the way, where instruction is seen as well as heard.
Jesus asks that a person's yes be yes and their no be no.
In the parable a man who lists his fasts and tithes goes home less justified than one who only asks for mercy. Can a record of good deeds itself become the obstacle?
Jesus tells his followers that a city set on a hill cannot be hid, nor a candle put under a bushel.
Jesus tells the people to do what their teachers bid, but not to do after their works, for they say and do not.
Paul warns of those who have a form of godliness and deny the power thereof.
Isaiah confesses that all our righteousnesses are as filthy rags. What is left of a call to deeds when the best of them are judged like that?
Confucius says that the superior man is modest in his speech, but exceeds in his actions.
Dickinson says that a word, when it is said, just begins to live. Are words only metaphors of reality, or do some words act?
Jeremiah warns against trusting in lying words, repeated: the temple of the Lord, the temple of the Lord.
The psalm describes who shall abide: one who walks uprightly, works righteousness and speaks the truth in the heart.
Jesus tells his disciples, when they have done all that was commanded, to say: we are unprofitable servants. What attitude toward one's own good deeds keeps them acceptable?
The Qur'an asks those who enjoin righteousness on others whether they forget themselves.
Jesus expects to have the proverb quoted against himself: physician, heal thyself.
The Preacher advises: be not rash with thy mouth, and let thy words be few.
Paul calls his converts themselves his epistle, known and read of all men.
The Dhammapada has each man direct himself first to what is proper, and then teach others.
Mill warned that bad men need nothing more to compass their ends than that good men should look on and do nothing.
Paul gives this as the law of Christ fulfilled: bear ye one another's burdens.
Paul says that with the mouth confession is made unto salvation. What place has spoken profession in a faith, if this is not a cycle of words?
A short chapter of the Qur'an says man is in a state of loss, save those who believe and do good works.
Thoreau went to the woods because he wished to live deliberately, and not to discover at death that he had not lived.
Aristotle says that we become just by doing just acts, temperate by doing temperate acts.
Paul says that to give all one's goods to the poor, without charity, profits nothing. Can deeds, too, be a kind of mere words?
Luke tells of Joseph, a counsellor, a good man and a just, who had not consented to the counsel and deed of the others.
Jesus rebukes those who are exact about tithes of mint and anise and omit the weightier matters of judgment, mercy and faith.
Lao Tzu holds that sincere words are not fine, and fine words are not sincere.
John's letter says that if a man say 'I love God' and hateth his brother, he is a liar.
Lao Tzu puts fewness of words first: he who knows does not care to speak, and he who is ever ready to speak does not know.
Proverbs observes that he that hath knowledge spareth his words, and marks by this the man of understanding.
James calls the tongue a fire, a little member that boasts great things. Is fewness of words a discipline of speech, or a distrust of it?
